name: Eagle (Apollo 11 LM descent stage)
why: To land the first humans, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin, on the Moon and get them home safely.
science: Proved that people could land on the Moon, explore, and leave again. The crew brought home about 21.5 kg of rocks showing that the dark 'seas' are old volcanic lava.
story: I'm the bottom half of Eagle, the first spacecraft to carry people to the Moon's surface. On July 20, 1969, I touched down with less than a minute of landing fuel to spare. When the crew left, I stayed behind as their launch pad, and I've been here ever since.
funFact: A plaque on my leg says: 'Here men from the planet Earth first set foot upon the Moon, July 1969, A.D. We came in peace for all mankind.'

name: Apollo 11 Passive Seismic Experiment (EASEP)
why: To listen for moonquakes and meteorite hits and learn what the inside of the Moon is like.
science: It was the first seismometer set up on another world. It ran on solar power for a few weeks and showed scientists how to build the longer-lasting seismic stations that later Apollo crews left behind.
story: The Apollo 11 astronauts set me up a short walk from Eagle, and I started listening right away. I felt the Moon's tiny trembles and radioed them to Earth until I stopped answering commands in August 1969.
funFact: Small heaters warmed by radioactive plutonium kept me from freezing during the long, cold lunar night.

name: Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
why: To give scientists on Earth a mirror target so they could measure the distance to the Moon with lasers.
science: Laser pulses bounced off it show that the Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm (1.5 inches) a year, and they help test Einstein's theory of gravity.
story: I'm a panel of 100 special mirrors that the Apollo 11 crew set down in 1969. I don't need power, so I've never stopped working. Observatories on Earth still fire lasers at me and time how long the light takes to come back.
funFact: Each of my 100 mirrors is a 'corner cube' that sends light straight back to wherever it came from, the same trick a bike reflector uses.

name: Intrepid (Apollo 12 LM descent stage)
why: To show that astronauts could land precisely on a chosen spot, right next to the robot lander Surveyor 3.
science: Intrepid's pinpoint landing proved that later crews could aim for specific science targets. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean set up the first nuclear-powered science station and brought back pieces of Surveyor 3 to see how two and a half years on the Moon had changed them.
story: I carried Pete Conrad and Alan Bean to the Ocean of Storms in November 1969. I landed so precisely that the robot lander Surveyor 3 was a short walk away. Now I'm the second crewed landing stage ever left on the Moon.
funFact: When Pete Conrad, one of the shorter astronauts, hopped off my ladder, he joked: 'Whoopie! Man, that may have been a small one for Neil, but that's a long one for me.'

name: Apollo 12 ALSEP science station
why: To keep measuring moonquakes, magnetism and the solar wind for years after the astronauts went home.
science: Its seismometer discovered that the Moon keeps vibrating for an hour or more after an impact, because its dry, broken-up rock carries shaking very well. It also measured the solar wind and found a weak magnetic field frozen into the local rocks.
story: I was the first nuclear-powered science station on the Moon, running on a small plutonium generator. I listened to the Moon for almost eight years, sending data home day and night. In 1977 NASA switched me off to save money.
funFact: The fuel for my power generator got stuck in its carrying case, and Pete Conrad had to whack the case with a hammer so Alan Bean could pull it out.

name: Intrepid ascent stage impact (Apollo 12)
why: Once the astronauts were safely back in the command module, mission control crashed the empty top half of Intrepid into the Moon to make a test moonquake.
science: The Apollo 12 seismometer recorded the crash for nearly an hour, a big surprise to scientists. It showed that the Moon's outer layers are dry and broken up, letting vibrations echo for a long time.
story: I'm the top half of Intrepid. I carried Pete Conrad and Alan Bean back up to their command module, Yankee Clipper, then I was sent crashing back down at about 1.7 km per second. My crash was the first moonquake ever made on purpose.
funFact: Scientists said the Moon 'rang like a bell' after I hit.

name: Surveyor 3
why: To practice landing on the Moon and dig into its soil before astronauts went there.
science: Its scoop dug trenches up to 18 cm deep and showed the soil was firm enough to land and walk on. In 1969, Apollo 12 astronauts brought its TV camera and other parts back to Earth so scientists could see how the Moon's environment had affected them.
story: My landing engines didn't shut off in time, so I bounced and touched down three times before settling. Two and a half years later, Apollo 12's Intrepid landed less than 200 meters from me. Pete Conrad and Alan Bean walked over, took my picture, and cut off my TV camera to take home.
funFact: My TV camera is now on display at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum in Washington, D.C.

name: Apollo 13 S-IVB rocket stage impact
why: To crash the used-up third stage of the Saturn V rocket into the Moon as a big, precisely timed test signal for the Apollo 12 seismometer.
science: It was the first rocket stage crashed into the Moon on purpose. The Apollo 12 seismometer, about 135 km away, felt the Moon shake for hours, showing how well lunar rock carries vibrations.
story: I'm the third stage of the Saturn V that launched Apollo 13. I was already on my way to the Moon when an oxygen tank exploded on the astronauts' spacecraft. While the crew swung around the Moon to head safely home, I crashed into it.
funFact: I hit the Moon at about 2.6 km per second, more than 9,000 km per hour.

name: Antares (Apollo 14 LM descent stage)
why: To land Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell in the Fra Mauro hills, the target Apollo 13 never reached.
science: The crew collected about 42 kg of rocks, including breccias (rocks made of broken pieces glued together) thought to have been thrown out by the giant impact that made the Imbrium basin.
story: I carried Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell to Fra Mauro in February 1971, finishing the job Apollo 13 had to give up. Before landing, a faulty abort switch almost ended the mission, but engineers on Earth quickly wrote a workaround for my computer. Now I sit quietly in the hills where they explored.
funFact: Alan Shepard hit two golf balls near me, using a golf club head attached to the handle of a sample-collecting tool.

name: Apollo 14 ALSEP science station
why: To add a second long-lasting seismometer and other instruments, so moonquakes could be recorded from more than one place.
science: Together with the Apollo 12 station, it started the Apollo seismic network, which grew to four stations. Its active seismic experiment used small explosive 'thumps' to probe the layers of soil and rock just below the surface.
story: Edgar Mitchell set out a line of my sensors and walked along it, firing small charges from a 'thumper' to make tiny moonquakes. I listened for more than six years, until NASA turned all the Apollo stations off in 1977.
funFact: On this mission the astronauts pulled their tools around on a two-wheeled cart nicknamed the 'rickshaw', the only hand cart ever used on the Moon.

name: Apollo 14 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
why: To add a second laser mirror target, so scientists could measure both the Moon's distance and how it wobbles.
science: Ranging to several reflectors lets scientists measure the Moon's tiny wobbles, which gave evidence that the Moon has a liquid core.
story: I'm a twin of Apollo 11's reflector, with 100 mirror prisms of my own. I need no power and have no moving parts. More than 50 years later, laser beams from Earth still bounce off me and race back home.
funFact: A laser pulse takes about 2.5 seconds to travel from Earth to me and back.

name: Apollo 14 S-IVB rocket stage impact
why: To make a big, carefully timed thump for the Apollo 12 seismometer.
science: Its crash sent vibrations deep into the Moon, helping scientists measure how fast seismic waves travel through the lunar crust.
story: I'm the third stage of the Saturn V that launched Apollo 14. After sending the astronauts toward the Moon, I was steered to crash into it. I hit at about 2.5 km per second and blasted out a crater bigger than a tennis court.
funFact: I weighed about 14 tonnes when I hit, more than two African elephants.

name: Antares ascent stage impact (Apollo 14)
why: Once the crew was finished with it, it was crashed on purpose to make another test moonquake.
science: It hit between the Apollo 12 and Apollo 14 seismometers, so both stations recorded it, helping scientists map the Moon's outer layers.
story: I'm the top half of Antares. I lifted Alan Shepard and Edgar Mitchell off the Moon and back to their command module, Kitty Hawk. Then I was dropped back onto the Moon to make a moonquake for science.
funFact: I struck at a very shallow angle, only about 3.6 degrees above the horizon, like a stone skimming across a pond.

name: Falcon (Apollo 15 LM descent stage)
why: To carry Dave Scott and Jim Irwin, plus the first lunar rover, for a three-day stay at the foot of the Apennine Mountains.
science: The first of the longer 'J-missions', it let the crew explore much farther than before. They found the 'Genesis Rock', a piece of ancient lunar crust about 4 billion years old.
story: I carried Dave Scott and Jim Irwin to the edge of Hadley Rille, a long winding valley, in July 1971. I also brought the first car to the Moon, folded up against my side. The astronauts lived inside me for three days, longer than any crew before them.
funFact: Near me, Dave Scott dropped a hammer and a falcon feather at the same moment. With no air to slow the feather, they hit the ground together, just as Galileo predicted.

name: Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle
status: Parked forever where it filmed liftoff
why: To let astronauts drive much farther from their lander and carry more tools and rocks.
science: It carried Scott and Irwin about 28 km over three moonwalks, to the rim of Hadley Rille and the slopes of Mount Hadley Delta, places they could never have reached on foot.
story: I was the first car ever driven on another world. On my first drive my front-wheel steering didn't work, so the astronauts steered with my back wheels only. For my last job, I parked about 130 meters east of Falcon so my TV camera could show people on Earth the liftoff.
funFact: I weigh 210 kg, but in the Moon's weak gravity I'd feel about as heavy as 35 kg does on Earth.

name: Apollo 15 ALSEP science station
why: To add a third seismic station and measure how much heat flows out of the Moon's interior.
science: With the Apollo 12 and 14 stations it formed a triangle that could pinpoint where moonquakes happen. Many deep moonquakes turned out to be about 1,000 km down and to repeat in step with the tides raised by Earth's gravity.
story: Dave Scott and Jim Irwin set me up on the plains near Hadley Rille. My heat probes sat in holes drilled into the ground to feel the Moon's inner warmth. I sent data home for six years, until NASA switched me off in 1977.
funFact: The ground was so tough that drilling the holes for my heat probes was much harder than expected, and the probes didn't go as deep as planned.

name: Apollo 15 Laser Ranging Retroreflector
why: To give laser stations on Earth a bigger, brighter mirror target.
science: With 300 prisms, three times as many as Apollo 11's, it sends back the most light, so it is the reflector laser stations use most. Its data helps measure the Earth-Moon distance to within millimeters.
story: I'm the biggest of the Apollo laser mirrors, with 300 glass prisms. The Apollo 15 crew set me up in 1971, and I've been bouncing laser light back to Earth ever since. I need no batteries and no repairs.
funFact: By the time a laser beam from Earth reaches me, it has spread out to a couple of kilometers wide, so only a tiny fraction of its light hits my prisms.

name: Apollo 15 S-IVB rocket stage impact
why: To create a test moonquake for the Apollo 12 and 14 seismometers.
science: Two stations recorded the crash, helping scientists study the structure of the crust between them.
story: I'm the Saturn V third stage that pushed Apollo 15 toward the Moon. Then I was aimed at the Moon itself and hit the ground at about 2.6 km per second, the day before the astronauts landed.
funFact: My crash released about as much energy as 11 tonnes of TNT.

name: Falcon ascent stage impact (Apollo 15)
why: After carrying the crew back to orbit, it was crashed on purpose so the seismometers could feel it.
science: Its impact gave the three-station seismic network a known source, helping scientists calibrate their moonquake measurements.
story: I'm the top half of Falcon. I lifted Dave Scott and Jim Irwin off the Moon on August 2, 1971, while the rover's camera filmed us go. After they climbed back into the command module Endeavour, I was sent back down to crash about 90 km west of where I started.
funFact: My liftoff was the first one ever shown on live TV from the Moon's surface.

name: Orion (Apollo 16 LM descent stage)
status: Parked forever in the Descartes highlands
why: To land John Young and Charlie Duke in the Moon's bright highlands, where scientists expected to find volcanic rocks.
science: The rocks turned out to be mostly breccias made by meteorite impacts, not volcanoes. That surprise changed how scientists understood the lunar highlands.
story: I carried John Young and Charlie Duke to the Descartes highlands in April 1972. A problem with the command module's engine delayed my landing by almost six hours while mission control checked it was safe. The crew lived inside me for three days.
funFact: Charlie Duke left a photo of his family on the ground near me, with a message signed on the back.

name: Apollo 16 Lunar Roving Vehicle
status: Parked forever where it filmed liftoff
why: To carry John Young and Charlie Duke across the rugged highlands to places too far to walk to.
science: It drove about 27 km, taking the crew up Stone Mountain and to the rim of North Ray crater to collect rocks blasted out from deep below.
story: John Young gave me a 'Grand Prix' test drive, speeding and swerving while Charlie Duke filmed, so engineers could see how I handled. I bounced so much that my wheels sometimes left the ground. My last parking spot was about 80 meters east of Orion.
funFact: My wheels were made of woven steel piano wire with titanium treads, not rubber tires.

name: Apollo 16 ALSEP science station
why: To add a fourth seismic station, in the highlands, and measure heat coming from inside the Moon.
science: Its seismometer made the Apollo network four stations strong. Together they recorded thousands of moonquakes and meteorite impacts until 1977, helping reveal the Moon's layered interior: crust, mantle and a small core.
story: John Young and Charlie Duke set me up in the highlands. While working, John accidentally caught his foot on the cable to my heat-flow experiment and pulled it loose, so that instrument never worked. My seismometer kept listening until 1977.
funFact: My power came from a nuclear generator that turned heat from plutonium into electricity, so I kept working through the two-week lunar nights.

name: Apollo 16 S-IVB rocket stage impact
why: To make a known thump for the Apollo seismometers.
science: Radio tracking was lost before it hit, so its location had to be estimated from seismometer data. Decades later, cameras on NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter found its crater.
story: I'm the third stage of Apollo 16's Saturn V. A problem cut off my radio before I hit the Moon, so for decades nobody knew exactly where I'd crashed. Then the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter spotted my crater, and LROC scientists announced the find in 2016.
funFact: I was 'lost' on the Moon for more than 40 years before scientists found my crater.

name: Challenger (Apollo 17 LM descent stage)
why: To land Gene Cernan and geologist Harrison Schmitt in the Taurus-Littrow valley, the last stop of the Apollo program.
science: Schmitt, the only professional scientist to walk on the Moon, found orange soil made of tiny glass beads from ancient volcanic fire fountains. The crew brought back about 110 kg of samples, the most of any Apollo mission.
story: I was the last Apollo lunar module to land, carrying Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt in December 1972. They spent three days exploring the valley around me. When they left, Gene Cernan's were the last human footprints on the Moon, at least so far.
funFact: My plaque reads: 'Here man completed his first explorations of the Moon, December 1972 A.D. May the spirit of peace in which we came be reflected in the lives of all mankind.'

name: Apollo 17 Lunar Roving Vehicle
status: Parked forever where it filmed liftoff
why: To carry Cernan and Schmitt to the mountains and giant boulders at the edges of the Taurus-Littrow valley.
science: It drove about 36 km, the farthest of the three rovers, taking the crew to huge boulders that had rolled down from the mountains and to the orange-soil site at Shorty crater.
story: Gene Cernan accidentally knocked off part of my right rear fender, and my wheels started spraying the crew with dust. They fixed it with maps, tape and clamps. At the end, I parked about 140 meters east of Challenger, and my TV camera, steered from Houston, followed the ascent stage as it blasted off.
funFact: Gene Cernan drove me at about 18 km per hour going downhill, a Moon speed record.

name: Apollo 17 ALSEP science station
why: To measure heat flow, dust, gravity and the Moon's extremely thin atmosphere at the last Apollo site.
science: Its heat probes measured warmth leaking out of the Moon, and explosive charges set off after the crew left let its geophones map the layers beneath the valley.
story: Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt set me up in December 1972. On their drives they placed eight explosive packages, which mission control set off after the astronauts had gone so I could feel the blasts. I kept working until 1977.
funFact: My Lunar Surface Gravimeter was designed to sense gravitational waves, but a design mistake meant it could never be balanced properly.

name: Apollo 17 S-IVB rocket stage impact
why: To give the Apollo seismometer network one more big test signal.
science: Four seismic stations recorded the crash, helping scientists measure the structure of the Moon's crust.
story: I'm the third stage of the last Saturn V to carry astronauts to the Moon. After sending Apollo 17 on its way, I crashed into the Moon the day before the astronauts landed.
funFact: The Saturn V that launched me was the only one ever to lift off at night.

name: Challenger ascent stage impact (Apollo 17)
why: After the last moonwalkers were back in orbit, it was crashed to make one more test moonquake.
science: It hit about 10 km from the landing site, where the instruments the crew had left behind recorded the shaking and helped map the layers under the valley.
story: I'm the top half of Challenger. On December 14, 1972, I lifted the last Apollo moonwalkers off the surface while the rover's camera watched me rise into the black sky. The next day I was sent crashing back into the Moon about 10 km southwest of my launch spot.
funFact: I hit the Moon at about 1.67 km per second, almost sideways, just 4.9 degrees above the horizon.

name: Surveyor 1
why: To prove that NASA could land gently on the Moon and test whether the ground could hold up a spacecraft.
science: It showed that the Moon's surface was firm enough to support a lander, which was great news for Apollo. Its camera sent back 11,240 pictures.
story: I was the first American spacecraft to land gently on the Moon, on June 2, 1966. Engineers weren't sure if the ground was solid or a deep sea of dust. I landed on the first try, and my footpads sank in only a few centimeters.
funFact: I landed about four months after the Soviet Luna 9 made the very first soft landing on the Moon.

name: Surveyor 5
why: To test the ground in the Sea of Tranquility, near where Apollo 11 would later land, and find out what lunar soil is made of.
science: Its alpha-scattering instrument made the first chemical analysis of soil on another world, finding it was like basalt, a volcanic rock common on Earth.
story: On the way to the Moon, a leak in my engine system almost ruined my landing, so engineers on Earth invented a new landing plan in a hurry. I landed on a slope inside a small crater and sent home more than 19,000 pictures.
funFact: I'm only about 25 km from where Apollo 11 landed less than two years later.

name: Surveyor 6
why: To check Sinus Medii, near the center of the Moon's near side, as a possible Apollo landing site and study its soil.
science: It returned nearly 30,000 pictures and analyzed the soil's chemistry. Its short hop let scientists see how the ground reacted to rocket exhaust and judge its strength.
story: On November 17, 1967, engineers fired my engines for 2.5 seconds. I rose about 3 meters into the air and landed 2.4 meters away, becoming the first spacecraft ever to lift off from the Moon.
funFact: My hop let my camera look at my old landing spot from a new position, giving scientists 3-D views of the ground.

name: Surveyor 7
why: With the Apollo landing areas checked, the last Surveyor was sent to study the rugged highlands near the young, bright crater Tycho.
science: It found that highland soil has less iron than the soil of the dark 'seas', showing the Moon's highlands and lowlands are made of different rock.
story: I'm the last Surveyor, and the only one to land in the bright, rugged highlands, about 30 km north of the rim of Tycho crater. When my chemistry instrument got stuck, mission control used my robot scoop to push it down to the ground.
funFact: My camera spotted laser beams fired at me from observatories in Arizona and California, an early taste of the laser experiments Apollo would make famous.

name: Ranger 6 impact
why: To take close-up TV pictures of the Moon before crashing, to help plan human landings.
science: Its cameras failed, so it returned no pictures, but it reached its target in the Sea of Tranquility, showing a spacecraft could be steered accurately to the Moon. Fixing its problems helped Ranger 7 succeed.
story: I flew all the way to the Moon right on course, but my cameras never turned on. Investigators think they were damaged by an electrical spark during launch. I crashed into the Sea of Tranquility without sending a single picture.
funFact: Five years after I crashed, Apollo 11 landed in the same Sea of Tranquility.

name: Ranger 7 impact
why: To send back close-up pictures of the Moon before impact, to help plan human landings.
science: It sent 4,308 pictures in its last 17 minutes, showing details as small as half a meter, far sharper than any telescope on Earth could see.
story: After six Ranger failures in a row, I was NASA's first Ranger success. I took pictures all the way down until I crashed at 2.62 km per second.
funFact: The area where I hit was later named Mare Cognitum, which means 'the Sea that has become known'.

name: Ranger 8 impact
why: To photograph the Sea of Tranquility, a smooth area being considered for Apollo landings.
science: It sent 7,137 close-up pictures, helping NASA judge whether the Sea of Tranquility was a safe place to land.
story: I dove toward the Sea of Tranquility, taking pictures for the last 23 minutes of my flight. Four years later, Apollo 11 landed about 70 km from where I crashed.
funFact: I took more pictures than any other Ranger: 7,137.

name: Ranger 9 impact
why: To take close-up pictures of Alphonsus crater, which scientists thought might once have had volcanic activity.
science: It sent 5,814 pictures of the crater's floor and central peak, the most detailed views yet of a large lunar crater.
story: I was the last Ranger. As I fell into Alphonsus crater, TV networks showed my pictures live, with the words 'Live from the Moon' on screen.
funFact: I hit the Moon at about 2.67 km per second, roughly 9,600 km per hour.

name: LCROSS Centaur rocket stage impact
why: To slam an empty rocket stage into a permanently shadowed crater near the south pole and look for water ice in the debris.
science: The cloud of debris it threw up contained water ice and vapor, about 5.6% of the material by mass, showing that ice is hidden in the Moon's coldest, darkest craters.
story: I'm the empty Centaur upper stage of the rocket that launched LCROSS and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter. Instead of drifting in space, I was aimed at Cabeus crater, a place that never sees sunlight. I hit at about 2.5 km per second and blasted a plume of dust and ice up into the sunlight.
funFact: I weighed about 2,300 kg, about as much as a large SUV, and hit at about 9,000 km per hour.

name: LCROSS shepherding spacecraft impact
why: To watch the Centaur's crash up close and measure its debris cloud before crashing itself.
science: Its instruments looked into the plume and detected water vapor and ice along with other chemicals, giving strong evidence of water ice in a lunar polar crater.
story: I traveled to the Moon attached to the Centaur rocket stage. Before impact we separated, and I followed about four minutes behind. I spent my last minutes measuring the Centaur's debris cloud and radioing the data home, then I crashed into Cabeus too.
funFact: My whole mission was planned so that my most important science happened in the last four minutes of my life.

name: Ebb (GRAIL-A) impact
status: Impact site named for Sally Ride
why: To fly in tandem with its twin, Flow, and map the Moon's gravity in detail.
science: By measuring tiny changes in the distance between the twins, GRAIL made the highest-resolution gravity map of any world at the time. It showed the Moon's crust is thinner and more cracked by impacts than scientists expected.
story: I'm Ebb, one of two twin spacecraft. My twin Flow and I chased each other around the Moon for almost a year. When our fuel ran low, we were steered into a mountain near the north pole, and I hit first, less than a minute before Flow.
funFact: Fourth graders from Emily Dickinson Elementary School in Bozeman, Montana, won a contest to name us Ebb and Flow.

name: Flow (GRAIL-B) impact
status: Impact site named for Sally Ride
why: To fly in tandem with its twin, Ebb, and map the Moon's gravity in detail.
science: Students across the U.S. used cameras on the GRAIL spacecraft to choose and take pictures of the Moon, through the MoonKAM program led by astronaut Sally Ride.
story: I'm Flow, Ebb's twin. I followed Ebb around the Moon, and in the end I followed it down too, hitting the same mountain moments later. NASA named our crash site after Sally Ride, the first American woman in space.
funFact: We were crashed in a remote spot on purpose, so we could never fall onto historic places like the Apollo landing sites.

name: LADEE impact
status: Impact crater on the far side
why: To study the Moon's extremely thin atmosphere and find out whether dust floats above the surface.
science: It found neon, helium and argon in the Moon's thin atmosphere and measured a thin, lopsided cloud of dust kicked up by tiny meteorite impacts. It also tested beaming data home by laser at a record 622 megabits per second.
story: I launched from Wallops Island, Virginia, in 2013, the first Moon mission ever launched from there. I flew lower and lower to sniff the Moon's thin air, and when my fuel ran out I crashed into the far side at about 1.7 km per second.
funFact: My laser communication test sent data from the Moon at 622 megabits per second, faster than many home internet connections at the time.

name: Lunar Prospector impact
status: Crash site in a shadowed south polar crater
why: To map what the Moon is made of from orbit and look for signs of ice at the poles.
science: Its neutron spectrometer found extra hydrogen near both poles, a sign that water ice may be trapped in permanently shadowed craters. It also mapped the Moon's gravity and magnetic fields.
story: After mapping the Moon for a year and a half, I was steered into a dark crater near the south pole in July 1999. Scientists hoped my crash would splash up water vapor that telescopes could see, but no plume was spotted.
funFact: I carried a small capsule holding some of the ashes of Eugene Shoemaker, a planetary scientist who helped train Apollo astronauts in geology. The crater I hit was later named Shoemaker in his honor.
